items.followUp: How does increasing temperature affect the rate of evaporation?

rubric.why: Identifies how heating affects the motion of particles.
rubric.description: Explains that particles gain kinetic energy and move faster at higher temperature.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for increased kinetic energy or faster particle motion.

rubric.why: Connects faster particle motion to the asked-for effect on diffusion.
rubric.description: States that faster-moving particles diffuse more rapidly, so the rate of diffusion increases.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the increase in diffusion rate.

modelAnswer: An increase in temperature gives particles more kinetic energy.
They move faster and spread through one another more rapidly, so the rate of diffusion increases.

items.followUp: Write the reaction of chlorine with water and name its products.

rubric.why: Shows the reactants involved in the halogen-water reaction.
rubric.description: Identifies that halogens react with water; gives chlorine and water as reactants.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the reaction or its reactants.

rubric.why: Checks the products that result from the reaction.
rubric.description: States that chlorine forms hydrochloric acid and hypochlorous acid in water.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for both products; accept the correct equation Cl₂ + H₂O → HCl + HOCl.

modelAnswer: Chlorine reacts with water to form hydrochloric acid and hypochlorous acid.
Cl₂ + H₂O ⇌ HCl + HOCl

items.followUp: Why is the first ionization energy of magnesium greater than that of sodium?

rubric.why: Recognises the periodic comparison between the two elements.
rubric.description: Identifies that an alkaline earth metal and an alkali metal being compared are in the same period.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for noting the same-period comparison.

rubric.why: Explains why the outer electron is harder to remove.
rubric.description: States that alkaline earth metals have a stronger attraction between the nucleus and the outer electron, so more energy is needed to remove it.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct explanation involving nuclear charge, atomic size, or stronger attraction.

modelAnswer: Alkali metals and alkaline earth metals occur next to each other in the same period.
An alkaline earth metal has a greater nuclear charge and a smaller atomic radius, so its outer electron is held more strongly and requires more energy to remove.

items.followUp: Write any three characteristics of a compound.

rubric.why: Checks that compounds have a definite composition.
rubric.description: States that the elements in a compound are present in a fixed proportion or ratio.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for fixed or definite composition.

rubric.why: Checks that compound formation produces a substance with its own properties.
rubric.description: States that a compound has properties different from those of its constituent elements.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the different properties of a compound.

rubric.why: Distinguishes chemical separation from physical separation.
rubric.description: States that a compound can be separated into its elements only by chemical methods.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for separation by chemical methods, not ordinary physical methods.

rubric.why: Checks the uniform nature of a compound.
rubric.description: States that a compound is homogeneous or has uniform composition throughout.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for homogeneity.

rubric.why: Checks a characteristic physical property of pure compounds.
rubric.description: States that a compound has definite melting and boiling points.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for definite melting point, boiling point, or both.

modelAnswer: A compound has a definite composition: its elements are combined in a fixed ratio.
Its properties are different from the properties of its constituent elements.
It is homogeneous and has uniform composition throughout.
Its elements can be separated only by chemical methods, not by physical methods.
A pure compound has definite melting and boiling points.

items.followUp: Explain the formation of magnesium chloride by transfer of electrons.

rubric.why: Checks the definition of an ionic bond.
rubric.description: Defines an ionic bond as the electrostatic force of attraction between oppositely charged ions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the electrostatic attraction definition.

rubric.why: Checks the electron arrangements or the electron available for transfer.
rubric.description: Identifies that sodium has one electron in its outer shell and chlorine needs one electron to complete its outer shell.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correct outer-shell information or the transfer of one electron.

rubric.why: Checks the ions produced by electron transfer.
rubric.description: States that sodium loses an electron to form Na⁺ and chlorine gains it to form Cl⁻.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for both correctly charged ions.

rubric.why: Checks that the student connects the ions to the compound and bond.
rubric.description: Explains that electrostatic attraction between Na⁺ and Cl⁻ forms ionic NaCl.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the attraction between the ions forming NaCl.

modelAnswer: An ionic bond is the electrostatic force of attraction between oppositely charged ions.
A sodium atom has the electronic configuration 2,8,1, while a chlorine atom has 2,8,7.
Sodium transfers its one outer-shell electron to chlorine.
Sodium forms Na⁺ and chlorine forms Cl⁻; the electrostatic attraction between these ions forms NaCl.

items.followUp: State any three postulates of Bohr's atomic model.

rubric.why: Checks Bohr's proposed paths for electrons.
rubric.description: States that electrons revolve around the nucleus in circular orbits.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the circular-orbit postulate.

rubric.why: Checks that electrons can occupy only specified orbits.
rubric.description: States that electrons can revolve only in certain permitted orbits or energy levels.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the permitted-orbit postulate.

rubric.why: Checks the energy condition for an electron in an allowed orbit.
rubric.description: States that an electron in a permitted stationary orbit has a definite energy and does not radiate energy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for constant energy or no radiation in a stationary orbit.

rubric.why: Checks how electrons change energy levels.
rubric.description: States that energy is absorbed or emitted when an electron moves from one orbit to another.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for energy absorption or emission during an orbit change.

rubric.why: Checks the relative energies or naming of the orbits.
rubric.description: States that the orbits are designated as shells such as K, L and M, with energy increasing in the larger orbits.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correct shell naming or the increase of energy with orbit size.

modelAnswer: Electrons revolve around the nucleus in circular orbits.
Electrons can occupy only certain permitted orbits, called energy levels or shells.
An electron in a permitted stationary orbit has a definite energy and does not emit or absorb energy.
An electron absorbs or emits energy when it jumps from one permitted orbit to another.
The orbits are designated K, L, M and so on; the energy of an electron is greater in an orbit farther from the nucleus.

items.followUp: Define solubility and state how temperature affects the solubility of solids and gases.

rubric.why: Checks the central meaning of solubility.
rubric.description: Defines solubility as the maximum amount of solute that dissolves in a given amount of solvent to form a saturated solution.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the maximum-amount definition.

rubric.why: Checks the standard amount and temperature conditions in the definition.
rubric.description: Specifies 100 g of solvent and a particular temperature.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for including these conditions.

rubric.why: Checks the usual temperature effect on solid solutes.
rubric.description: States that the solubility of most solids in liquids increases as temperature rises.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the usual increase for solids.

rubric.why: Checks the contrasting effect of temperature on gases.
rubric.description: States that gas solubility in liquids generally decreases as temperature rises.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the decrease in gas solubility.

modelAnswer: Solubility is the maximum amount of solute that dissolves in 100 g of a solvent at a particular temperature to form a saturated solution.
The solubility of most solid solutes in liquids increases with an increase in temperature.
The solubility of gases in liquids generally decreases with an increase in temperature.

items.followUp: Define one atomic mass unit in terms of the carbon-12 atom.

rubric.why: Checks the fractional definition of the unit.
rubric.description: States that one atomic mass unit is one-twelfth of a reference atom's mass.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the one-twelfth fraction.

rubric.why: Checks that the correct reference atom is named.
rubric.description: Identifies the reference as a carbon-12 atom.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming carbon-12.

modelAnswer: One atomic mass unit (amu) is defined as one-twelfth of the mass of one carbon-12 atom.
